presentingComplaint: Malaise, swelling of the legs and face, and dark urine for 2 weeks, with reduced urine output over the last 3 days.
history: A 52-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of progressive fatigue, anorexia, and puffiness around the eyes on waking, followed by bilateral ankle swelling. He describes tea-coloured (dark) urine and a marked reduction in urine volume over the last 3 days. He denies dysuria or frank haematuria clots. He reports occasional low-grade fevers, arthralgias, and a faint rash on the lower legs about 3 weeks ago that has since resolved. No recent sore throat or skin infection. No haemoptysis, sinus symptoms, or epistaxis. No prior renal disease, no NSAID use. No known diabetes or hypertension previously. Non-smoker, no significant alcohol use.
examination: Alert, mildly unwell-appearing man. Periorbital and bilateral pitting pedal oedema present. No skin rash currently, no palpable purpura. Chest clear, no crepitations. Cardiovascular exam unremarkable, no pericardial rub. No joint swelling. No oral ulcers or nasal crusting. Abdomen soft, no organomegaly.
imaging: Renal ultrasound: normal-sized kidneys, no obstruction, preserved corticomedullary differentiation
Chest X-ray: no infiltrates, no pulmonary haemorrhage
differentialDiagnoses: IgA nephropathy / IgA vasculitis with rapid progression
finalDiagnosis: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (ANCA-associated, pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis) with acute kidney injury
citations: Harrison 22e — Glomerular Diseases: Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis
KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Glomerular Diseases 2021
KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for ANCA-Associated Vasculitis 2024
contraindications: Avoid nephrotoxic agents (NSAIDs, IV contrast unless essential, aminoglycosides)
High-dose glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide/rituximab require infection screening (latent TB, hepatitis B) before immunosuppression
Avoid delay in renal biopsy unless contraindicated (uncontrolled bleeding risk, single functioning kidney, uncontrolled severe hypertension) as timely diagnosis dictates urgent immunosuppression
edgeCases: If anti-GBM antibodies were positive instead, plasma exchange becomes mandatory in addition to immunosuppression
Pulmonary-renal syndrome (diffuse alveolar haemorrhage) can coexist with ANCA-associated RPGN and changes urgency/ICU triage
Normal complement with positive ANCA favours pauci-immune GN over post-infectious (low C3/C4) or lupus (low C3/C4, positive ANA/dsDNA) GN

'aki' is listed separately in the disease vocabulary as a distinct diagnosable entity; this case is a glomerulonephritis-driven AKI, so 'glomerulonephritis' is the primary acceptable id, with 'aki' as a reasonable differential/downstream id since renal function is acutely deteriorating
expectedMaiK: MaiK should flag rapidly rising creatinine with active urinary sediment (dysmorphic RBCs/RBC casts) as RPGN until proven otherwise, prioritize urgent nephrology referral and renal biopsy, and note ANCA/anti-GBM/complement/ANA serologies as first-line workup before empirical immunosuppression.
